articles.title: AI reveals explosive bursts in bird evolution
articles.summary: Songbirds appear to have evolved through rare explosions of change separated by long periods of slower development. Many of those bursts lined up with major climate shifts, suggesting that environmental upheaval can reshape life in powerful ways.
articles.content:
University of Michigan scientists have used artificial intelligence to uncover a striking pattern in the evolution of Passeriformes, the vast bird group that includes most songbirds. Their analysis suggests these birds did not evolve at a steady pace. Instead, major changes often arrived in rapid bursts that lined up with shifts in Earth's climate.

Evolutionary theory has long proposed that life diversifies through periods of fast change followed by slower phases. Fossils have offered clues that this pattern exists, but the new study identified it by analyzing skeletal measurements from modern bird specimens. The researchers also found that several of the most important evolutionary bursts occurred around periods of major climate change.

Evolution in Sudden Bursts

"This is really important for evolutionary theory because there's a long history, going back 100 years, that predicts the emergence of new groups, called evolutionary radiations, is often associated with an explosive burst of diversification. Evolutionary theory predicts that adaptive radiations may account for a large portion of the diversity of life on Earth," said Jake Berv, lead author of the study and postdoctoral fellow in the U-M School for Environment and Sustainability.

"This could be because of a new ecological opportunity, or it could be because a group dispersed to a new continent, resulting in dramatic accelerations in their rate of evolution. The idea is that, over time, there's less opportunity as evolution proceeds, and so it slows down, and that this occurs in pulses across time. That's what theory predicts, and that seems to be what we see in the data as well."

The results were produced with artificial intelligence and a large statistical model. The findings are published in Nature Ecology & Evolution and were primarily supported by Schmidt Sciences and the David and Lucile Packard Foundation.

AI Measures Thousands of Bird Skeletons

To reconstruct the evolutionary history of passerines, the University of Michigan team, including senior author Brian Weeks, studied more than 2,000 species and assembled over 170,000 individual skeletal measurements.

Collecting data at that scale was possible because of Skelevision, an AI tool developed by Weeks' laboratory in collaboration with David Fouhey's laboratory at New York University.

Skelevision photographs specimens, which in this case were bird skeletons, in front of a grid that provides a consistent measurement scale. During a seven-year collaboration, Weeks and Fouhey created an AI model capable of accurately measuring 12 bones across a bird's skeleton.

The researchers used the system to scan and measure more than 15,000 museum specimens. Most came from the collections of the U-M Museum of Zoology. Each specimen can be scanned in about 45 seconds, allowing researchers to digitize entire museum collections far more efficiently than would otherwise be possible.

Reconstructing 45 Million Years of Change

Berv also created a new statistical method called bifrost, which allowed the team to analyze each species' complete skeleton rather than examining individual bones in isolation. Using this approach, the researchers estimated how passerine body shapes changed over roughly 45 million years of evolution.

"The whole organism is an integrated, complex morphology, and each of the individual pieces is interrelated to every other part in the body," Berv said. "The question from the model's perspective is, 'What is the sequence of evolutionary changes that needs to happen to explain the variation we can see today?'"

The analysis revealed a period of especially rapid body-shape evolution around 35 million years ago. This burst coincided with the Eocene-Oligocene transition, a period marked by intense global cooling.

The statistical results also identified a cluster of evolutionary slowdowns around 15 million years ago, which coincided with another major geological event.

"Our findings have definitely shifted my thinking about how the world works," said Weeks, associate professor of ecosystem science and management at U-M's School for Environment and Sustainability. "This pattern we found with rare, big increases in the rates of evolution and lots of small decreases in the rate of evolution is really consistent with a pattern where lineages are exploring new ecological space and changing rapidly to take advantage of that opportunity."

Climate and Geography Shape Evolution

The researchers then tested the pattern by analyzing the global distribution of the birds in their dataset. They found that geography also helps predict the average rate of morphological evolution.

Bird communities at more extreme latitudes, where seasonal temperatures vary more sharply, tend to include species that evolve faster than those living closer to the equator. Because similar patterns appeared both across millions of years and across modern geographic regions, the findings suggest environmental variability may play an important role in driving changes in body shape.

"It looks like there's a connection between latitudinal gradients and rates of morphological evolution that has been underappreciated," Weeks said. "I hope our findings will inspire a new integration of rates of morphological change into other big areas of interest, things like the very well-known latitudinal gradients in biodiversity."

Museum Collections Gain New Value Through AI

The work also highlights the scientific importance of museum collections. According to Weeks, artificial intelligence is making it possible to extract information from preserved specimens at a scale that would have been difficult to imagine in the past.

"It's especially clear how important it is to invest in museums when you think about the scale of an analysis like this; it's so far beyond the scope of what can be done using specimens contributed by an individual collector," he said. "It's also fun to imagine what early collectors would make of how we're using the specimens they collected -- I imagine it would blow their minds to learn that a computer has analyzed a photograph of these specimens. It's just another example of how impossible it is to foresee the full future value of a specimen."

Lessons for Modern Climate Change

The researchers say the findings may also help scientists think about how species could respond to the rapid climate changes now unfolding around the world.

"Right now, we're in this moment in human history where there's dramatic global climate change, and we don't know what's going to happen over even a 10-year period, let alone over a 10-million-year period," Berv said. "To have a chance of understanding the long-term impact of human activity on Earth, we have to study the relationship between events in Earth's history and evolutionary transitions."

The research was also supported by the Michigan Institute for Data & AI in Society, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, and the National Science Foundation.

articles.title: Demand for lithium is surging: here’s how to make mining more sustainable
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02195-zResearchers are looking for ways to extract the metal from underground reservoirs that use less water.
articles.content:
Lithium salts being recovered from brine pools in South America.Credit: Martin Bernetti/AFP via Getty

As more people seek out electric vehicles and batteries to store renewable energy, demand for lithium, the metal at the core of most rechargeable batteries, is intensifying. But mining lithium has substantial impacts on the environment. A wave of innovative technologies could make its extraction more sustainable.

Electric vehicles accounted for more than one-quarter of all global car sales last year, according to the International Energy Agency. The agency projects that demand for lithium for electric vehicles could reach around 665 kilotonnes by 2035. Yet, planned and existing mining projects would produce only about 450 kilotonnes, leaving a substantial gap if production capacity does not increase.

Demand for lithium batteries for energy-storage capacity for renewable electricity will put further pressure on lithium production, says Zhikao Li, a chemical and biological engineer at Monash University.

About 25% of this lithium is projected to come from parts of Chile and Argentina. Here, producers pump naturally occurring lithium-rich brine from underground aquifers into large evaporation ponds. Over a period of months or years, sunlight and wind concentrate the brine until lithium-rich salts can be recovered. The process is effective, but inefficient, say scientists. Brine contains many dissolved salts, each with distinct solubilities. As the water evaporates, the least soluble salts crystallize first, whereas lithium salts are some of the last to separate. Up to 50% of the lithium can be left behind in evaporation ponds, and extra fresh water is often needed to purify the remaining metal.

“The key limitation for existing processes is the fresh water, and also it’s a very slow process,” says Huanting Wang, who is working on alternative extraction methods at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia.

The water use is particularly concerning because brine deposits tend to exist in arid or semi-arid regions where fresh water is already scarce, says Ehsan Vahidi, a who studies metallurgical engineering at the University of Nevada in Reno.

Brine mining has impacts for local Indigenous communities and damages wetland ecosystems, say researchers.

Greener alternatives

Direct lithium extraction is an alternative method that research teams and companies are exploring. These systems use membranes, solvents and electrochemical processes to selectively remove lithium ions from brine.

One possible strategy is being developed by Wang's team at Monash University. The team began by evaporating the brine so that it formed a solid salt mixture and then used acetone and ethanol to selectively dissolve lithium salts while leaving most other compounds behind. In a laboratory study published last month, they report that the process recovered around 95% of the lithium present1.

The method substantially reduces freshwater use compared to traditional methods, the researchers say. And the method could be coupled with solar-powered systems that capture and condense the evaporated water, allowing it to be recycled instead of being lost to the atmosphere. The solvents could also be recovered and reused.

Wang says that the technique could eventually be used to recover lithium present in industrial waste streams and mining residues, which are otherwise wasted.

Peter Sherrell, a materials scientist at RMIT University, Melbourne, says this approach has several advantages over existing methods, such as the high rate of lithium recovery and the fact that the solvents can be recovered and reused. But whether the industry will invest in the technology so it can be used in the real world remains to be seen, he adds.
articles.reasoning: The article discusses innovative technologies that could make lithium mining more sustainable, reducing freshwater use and environmental harm while meeting growing demand for electric vehicle batteries and renewable energy storage. This represents a significant positive impact on environmental conservation and resource management with broad societal benefits.

articles.title: Reducing Waste: Your Citizen-and-Voter Playbook
articles.summary:
Our ability to reuse, repair, and recycle is determined in city halls, state capitals, and...
The post Reducing Waste: Your Citizen-and-Voter Playbook appeared first on Earth911.
articles.content:
Our ability to reuse, repair, and recycle is determined in city halls, state capitals, and Washington, D.C. The solution to food rotting before it’s eaten, flexible film that curbside will never touch, 81 pounds of textiles per person per year, electronics leaching heavy metals, diapers outlasting the children who wore them start at the ballot box.

The recycling access gap the EPA identified is not a personal-responsibility problem. Forty percent of U.S. households lack curbside recycling service — six percent have no access to recycling at all — but almost all enjoy trash pickup services. Six percent have no recycling service at all. The gap between what the existing infrastructure does and what it could do represents $36.5 to $43.4 billion in unspent public investment — funding the Environmental Protection Agency’s 2024 assessment found would raise the national recycling rate from 32% to 61% and pay for itself through avoided disposal costs alone.

The choice to make or not make that investment is a political choice. That is what elections and comment periods and city council meetings are for. Dig into our guide to voting for the creation of a robust U.S. circular economy. We offer suggestions about how to vote on a couple of specific issues, but our goal is to help you think through how your community needs to change, what ideas to present to your representatives, and the evidence to share when you talk with them.

At the local level: what elected officials can do

Municipal governments make the decisions that determine your household’s recycling access. City councils approve solid-waste contracts. County commissioners determine whether a composting facility gets funded. Public works departments decide whether drop-off sites stay open. These officials respond to constituent pressure more reliably than almost any other level of government.

Ask specific questions

“Does our city have a plan to expand curbside organics collection?” is a question a public works director can answer. “What’s our current MRF contract, and when does it come up for renewal?” is a question a city councilmember can put on an agenda. “Is the municipality pursuing federal infrastructure funding for recycling facility upgrades?” is a question that can unlock a grant application that would otherwise not get filed. Citizens, who ultimately determine who sits on local councils, have their greatest impact near home.

Federal infrastructure money for recycling and composting exists but is underutilized. The EPA’s 2024 assessment found that 48% of states and territories don’t even collect data on how many curbside programs they have. You cannot pursue federal funding for something you haven’t quantified. Pushing local officials to measure a gap in services is the first step in the path to closing it.

Know your tipping fee and what’s driving it

The national average landfill tipping fee reached $62.28 per ton in 2024, up 10% from the prior year, the steepest annual jump in more than a decade. Cities in the Northeast pay over $80 per ton on average. As disposal costs rise, the cost-benefit argument for recycling and composting programs improves automatically. Local officials who have not recalculated their waste management economics recently may be working with outdated numbers. Ask them to run the comparison and explain to the community how they plan to improve services while raising rates.

At the state level: learn where your state is on the EPR map

Extended producer responsibility (EPR) laws that shift recycling infrastructure costs to the producers of packaging and products is the most consequential policy lever currently available. The state-by-state EPR map maintained by the Product Stewardship Institute shows where laws have passed, where bills are active, and where the gap remains. Where you live determines what producers must contribute to the cost of collection and processing, or face penalties.

Packaging EPR programs now cover most of the West Coast and Northeast

Oregon launched its program on July 1, 2025, with roughly $200 million in annual producer funding and posted first-year results earlier this month . The state added 20 new recycling centers, distributed tens of thousand of new bins, and gave more than 600,000 citizens new access to collection sites within 15 miles of their homes.

Maine, Colorado, Minnesota, and Maryland have laws in various stages of build-out. California’s program is projected to activate in 2027. And Washington signed the Recycling Reform Act in 2025, and the state’s Recycling Reform Act requires producers to fund 90% of recycling system costs statewide by 2030.

If you live in one of these states, find out how the program works. Holding producers accountable and pushing for strong performance requirements, particularly on flexible plastics, can change the environmental impact your taxes fund. If your state has no packaging EPR law, as in New York, where a bill failed again in 2026 after three attempts, send mail to your House and Senate representatives that makes a specific request for action. Check the Recycling Partnership’s EPR toolkit and the Product Stewardship Institute’s 2026 legislative tracker to find active bills by state and connect their advocates to testimony opportunities. Citizens who found and contacted the legislative sponsor of EPR bills and showe up for a committee hearing have helped packaging EPR laws go from a dream to reality in every state where bills have passed.

Bottle bills: the most effective way to boost container recovery

Deposit-return-scheme states recover container glass and aluminum at roughly twice the rate of states without bottle bills. Seven states introduced bottle-bill legislation in 2026, including Washington’s HB 1607, Maryland’s HB 331, Massachusetts’ H3464, and New York’s bill to double the deposit to 10 cents. If your state has a bill in session, a constituent email or committee appearance during the session window is the most direct action available.

Textile EPR: California leads, every other state needs to follow

Textile EPR exists in one state, California. SB 707, the Responsible Textile Recovery Act, led to the March 2026 selection of Landbell USA as the producer responsibility organization that will run the statewide clothing and textiles collection program. Every other state with a fast-fashion retail presence and that contributes to the 17-million-ton national textile waste stream is a ripe target for your personal advocacy. Track the program’s rollout and learn about the issues your legislator needs to understand by visiting the SB 707 implementation tracker.

State-level social cost of carbon accounting.

California, Colorado, and New York have maintained their own social cost of carbon (SCC) frameworks independent of the federal rollback ordered in Executive Order 14154. These systems calculate the future cost, in terms of health and environmental damage, of a ton of carbon. Setting that price enables states to levy penalties to cover the expenses associated with climate change and extreme weather.

States without their own frameworks effectively treat climate damage as a give-away, which produces systematically wrong answers on every cost-benefit analysis related to waste. Advocating for state-level SCC adoption is unglamorous work, and that’s why it matters most; it can shift the entire regulatory calculus for waste, energy, and transportation with one bill. The Resources for the Future SCC explainer is the great resource for making the case to state legislators.

At the federal level: what to watch and what to fight

Federal policy shapes what the states can do, what data exists to make the case, and what producers are required to account for. The EU has pursued regulation much more aggressively than the United States, but consumer demand for environmental accountability and impact data is on the rise.

Fight the elimination of the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program

In September 2025, EPA formally proposed ending the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program, the facility-level emissions tracking system that provides the data researchers use to measure the gap between reported and actual landfill methane emissions. The formal rulemaking drew 53,085 public comments before its November 2025 deadline. The rule has not been finalized. Satellite measurements suggest actual landfill methane emissions average roughly six times what facilities report under the current program; eliminating reporting doesn’t reduce emissions, it removes accountability. Contact your senators and Congressional representative and share your opinion about how the rule should be finalized.

Federal infrastructure funding for recycling exists and can be expanded

The EPA’s $36.5–$43.4 billion infrastructure investment estimate describes the cost of closing the access gap. It’s not necessary to leave this to the states, and a national system can create efficiencies that reduce producers’ cost of compliance.

Congressional appropriations and infrastructure funding both have pathways to recycling investment. The recycling industry generates $184 billion in annual economic activity and supports 603,000 jobs directly and indirectly. Ask your federal representatives if they are willing to treat recycling infrastructure is domestic industrial policy, even as a national security investment to reduce dependence on overseas sources. Don’t just ask, take the time to recycle to demonstrate the demand through your curbside bin.

Ask candidates what they actually know

A candidate who thinks the recycling system is working because they have a blue bin has not looked at the numbers. Here are four questions worth putting to candidates at every level:

What is the recycling access gap in your district, and what is your plan to close it?

Does the state have packaging EPR legislation, and if not, why not? (Check the PSI legislative tracker for your state’s status.)

What is your position on the social cost of carbon as a tool for making regulatory decisions?

How would you vote on federal infrastructure funding for materials recovery (recycling) and organics processing (composting)?

Their answers reveal whether waste policy is something the candidate has thought about or something they are about to learn they need to think about.

The system is not broken because people don’t care enough about recycling — it is broken because the infrastructure was never built, the producers were never made responsible, and the accounting has never been honest. Those are fixable problems, and the people with the power to fix them are accountable to you.

articles.title: What India’s hydrogen train launch means for its vast railway network
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM India launched its first hydrogen-powered train earlier this month. It was built domestically and is now operating in Haryana. Two hydrogen-powered driving cars, eight passenger coaches, a capacity of about 2,600 passengers, and a top speed of 47 mph (75 kph). Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the train, called […]
The post What India’s hydrogen train launch means for its vast railway network first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

India launched its first hydrogen-powered train earlier this month. It was built domestically and is now operating in Haryana. Two hydrogen-powered driving cars, eight passenger coaches, a capacity of about 2,600 passengers, and a top speed of 47 mph (75 kph).

Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the train, called the “NaMo Green Rail,” at Jind railway station. The name is a common abbreviation of Modi’s first and last names. “This is a very significant day in the direction of self-reliant India and sustainable development,” he said.

The chemistry

Hydrogen fuel cells generate electricity by combining hydrogen and oxygen. The only direct emission is water vapor. The pilot includes hydrogen storage and refueling infrastructure to test how the technology performs in India’s rail network before any wider rollout.

What it’s replacing

India’s rail network is one of the world’s largest. Not all of it is electrified, and diesel powers most of the unelectrified routes. Hydrogen replaces diesel without requiring those lines to be fully electrified first. Several other countries have already deployed hydrogen trains on similar routes.

The net-zero picture

India has committed to net-zero emissions by 2070. The hydrogen rail push is part of a broader national effort to develop green hydrogen domestically, cut carbon from heavy transport, and reduce fuel import dependency.

Friday’s launch is a pilot. The storage and refueling infrastructure being tested alongside the train will determine how far the approach can scale.

articles.personality_title: India launches its first hydrogen-powered train to cut rail emissions
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – India has one of the largest railway networks in the world. Most trains run on diesel, especially on routes that are not fully electrified. To reduce pollution and reliance on diesel, India is exploring cleaner fuel options.

**What happened** – Earlier this month, India introduced its first hydrogen-powered train called the “NaMo Green Rail.” It was built in India and started running in the state of Haryana. The train has two hydrogen-powered engines, eight passenger coaches, and can carry about 2,600 people at speeds up to 47 miles per hour (75 kilometers per hour). Prime Minister Narendra Modi officially launched the train at Jind railway station.

**Impact** – This train uses hydrogen fuel cells that produce electricity by combining hydrogen and oxygen, releasing only water vapor as exhaust. This reduces harmful emissions compared to diesel trains. Since not all tracks are electrified, hydrogen trains can replace diesel ones without needing expensive electric wires everywhere. This pilot project also tests hydrogen storage and refueling systems, important for future expansion.

**What's next step** – The success of this pilot will help decide if hydrogen trains can be used widely across India’s rail network. It fits into India’s goal to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2070 and reduce fuel imports. If the technology works well, more hydrogen trains and refueling stations could be built to make train travel cleaner nationwide.

**One-sentence takeaway** – India’s first hydrogen-powered train marks a promising step toward cleaner, more sustainable rail travel across the country.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’Inde lance son premier train à hydrogène pour réduire les émissions ferroviaires
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L’Inde possède l’un des plus grands réseaux ferroviaires au monde. La plupart des trains fonctionnent au diesel, surtout sur les lignes non électrifiées. Pour réduire la pollution et la dépendance au diesel, l’Inde explore des options de carburant plus propres.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Ce mois-ci, l’Inde a présenté son premier train à hydrogène appelé « NaMo Green Rail ». Il a été construit en Inde et circule dans l’État de Haryana. Le train comprend deux moteurs à hydrogène, huit wagons passagers, et peut transporter environ 2 600 personnes à une vitesse maximale de 75 kilomètres par heure. Le Premier ministre Narendra Modi a inauguré le train à la gare de Jind.

**Impact** – Ce train utilise des piles à combustible à hydrogène qui produisent de l’électricité en combinant hydrogène et oxygène, ne rejetant que de la vapeur d’eau. Cela réduit les émissions nocives par rapport aux trains diesel. Comme toutes les voies ne sont pas électrifiées, les trains à hydrogène peuvent remplacer les trains diesel sans besoin de câbles électriques coûteux partout. Ce projet pilote teste aussi les systèmes de stockage et de ravitaillement en hydrogène, essentiels pour un déploiement futur.

**Prochaine étape** – Le succès de ce projet pilote aidera à décider si les trains à hydrogène peuvent être largement utilisés sur le réseau ferroviaire indien. Cela s’inscrit dans l’objectif de l’Inde d’atteindre zéro émission nette de carbone d’ici 2070 et de réduire les importations de carburant. Si la technologie fonctionne bien, plus de trains à hydrogène et de stations de ravitaillement pourraient être construits pour rendre le transport ferroviaire plus propre.

**Une phrase clé** – Le premier train à hydrogène de l’Inde est une avancée prometteuse vers un voyage ferroviaire plus propre et durable à travers le pays.
articles.personality_title_es: India lanza su primer tren impulsado por hidrógeno para reducir emisiones ferroviarias
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – India tiene una de las redes ferroviarias más grandes del mundo. La mayoría de los trenes funcionan con diésel, especialmente en rutas que no están electrificadas. Para reducir la contaminación y la dependencia del diésel, India está buscando opciones de combustible más limpias.

**Qué pasó** – A principios de este mes, India presentó su primer tren impulsado por hidrógeno llamado “NaMo Green Rail”. Fue construido en India y comenzó a operar en el estado de Haryana. El tren tiene dos motores a hidrógeno, ocho vagones para pasajeros y puede transportar alrededor de 2,600 personas a una velocidad máxima de 75 kilómetros por hora (47 millas por hora). El primer ministro Narendra Modi inauguró el tren en la estación de Jind.

**Impacto** – Este tren utiliza pilas de combustible de hidrógeno que generan electricidad al combinar hidrógeno y oxígeno, liberando solo vapor de agua. Esto reduce las emisiones dañinas en comparación con los trenes diésel. Como no todas las vías están electrificadas, los trenes de hidrógeno pueden reemplazar a los de diésel sin necesidad de instalar cables eléctricos en todas partes. Este proyecto piloto también prueba sistemas de almacenamiento y abastecimiento de hidrógeno, importantes para una expansión futura.

**Próximo paso** – El éxito de este piloto ayudará a decidir si los trenes de hidrógeno pueden usarse ampliamente en la red ferroviaria de India. Esto forma parte del objetivo de India de alcanzar emisiones netas cero para 2070 y reducir la importación de combustibles. Si la tecnología funciona bien, podrían construirse más trenes y estaciones de abastecimiento de hidrógeno para hacer que el transporte ferroviario sea más limpio en todo el país.

**Una frase clave** – El primer tren impulsado por hidrógeno de India es un paso prometedor hacia un viaje en tren más limpio y sostenible en todo el país.
